# CLAUDE.md - Bot Instructions

## Project Structure

This project uses **two separate jj-git repos**:

1. **App repo** (`/` — project root): Contains the application source code.
2. **Bot session repo** (`/.claude/`): Contains Claude Code session data.

Both repos are managed with `jj` (Jujutsu), which coexists with git.

## Repo Paths (relative from project root)

- App repo: `.` (project root)
- Bot session repo: `.claude`
  (symlink from `~/.claude/projects/<path-to-project-root>/.claude`)

## Working Directory

Prefer staying in the project root. Use `-R` flags or absolute paths
to target other directories rather than `cd`. If `cd` seems necessary,
discuss with the user first — losing track of cwd causes subtle
command failures downstream.

When invoking shell commands, prefer the shortest unambiguous path —
usually relative to cwd (`ls notes/`, not
`ls /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/notes/`). Long absolute paths
clutter the transcript without adding information. Out-of-workspace
paths (`/tmp/...`, `~/.config/...`) stay absolute. Read/Edit/Write
tool args also stay absolute — that's a tool-boundary constraint,
not a stylistic choice.

## Memory

Do not use the bot's per-project memory directory
(`~/.claude/projects/<path>/memory/`). In a dual-repo setup with
CLAUDE.md it provides no capability CLAUDE.md doesn't already cover,
and it loses on discoverability:

- **CLAUDE.md** — at the repo root, a well-known location for bot
  instructions, committed, reviewable, visible to every collaborator
  (human or bot).
- **Memory directory** — hidden under the user's home, tied to one
  machine, invisible to anyone but the bot, never diffed or reviewed.

Easy for everyone to find beats convenient for the bot alone. Put
durable context in CLAUDE.md (or committed `notes/`) instead.

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes — CLAUDE.md, `notes/`, commit bodies,
chores sections — should stick to observations and direct descriptions
of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal claim
enters the text, prefix it with "The bot thinks ..." so a reader can
tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader
(or the bot on a later session) can pick it up as a known fact when
it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction worth keeping visible
in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no
marker. Prefix with "The bot thinks ..." (or a close variant like
"The bot's guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins
because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal
state"), a prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any
reasoning not directly supported by the data on hand.

## Committing

Use `-R` (`--repository`) at the end to target the correct repo. Use
relative paths to reduce noise. Putting `-R` last keeps the verb/action
visible at the start of the command.

### App repo
```
jj commit -m \
"title" \
-m "body

ochid: /.claude/<changeID>" \
-R .
```

### Bot session repo
```
jj commit -m \
"title" \
-m "body

ochid: /<changeID>" \
-R .claude
```

## jj Basics

- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude` — show working copy status
- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude` — show commit log
- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — finalize working copy into a commit
- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — set description without committing
- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>` — push a bookmark (no
  `--allow-new` flag; jj pushes new bookmarks without special flags)
- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited.
  `jj commit` finalizes it and creates a new empty working copy on top.
- The `.claude` repo always has uncommitted changes during an active
  session because session data updates continuously.

## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one shape: a short intro
that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet
list for the details. Wrap lines at ≤72 cols (bullet continuations
indent two spaces). Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs — they hide the
structure that bullets make scannable.

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files —
  see [Doc comments](#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both app-repo and session-repo). The
  ≤50-col title is the commit-specific add-on; see
  [Commit Message Style](#commit-message-style).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores-NN.md` — see
  [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo and Done entries in `notes/todo.md` when an entry needs more
  than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies** — bullets are file-by-file: one bullet per file
  changed, file plus a one-line gist (e.g.
  `README.md: new Overview intro`). Source of truth for the
  mechanical edit list.
- **Chores / todo / done** — bullets are conceptual (design points,
  structural notes, the "what landed and why" at a notch above
  file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list —
  see [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments** — bullets are whatever structure fits (fields,
  cases, invariants).

## Commit Message Style

Use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) with
a version suffix:

```
<type>: <short description> (<version>)
```

- **Title**: ≤50 chars (the "50" of the git 50/72 rule), a short
  summary of *what* changed. The version suffix counts toward the
  50 — the descriptive part gets whatever's left after `<type>: `
  and ` (<version>)`, so favor terse phrasings (`port X to Context`
  over `X → Context + XParams`) when the names run long. Common
  types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`.
- **Body**: [Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets), wrap
  ≤72 (the "72" of the 50/72 rule). App-repo bullets are
  **file-by-file** — one bullet per file changed, file plus a
  one-line gist. This list **is the source of truth** for the
  cycle's mechanical change record; chores carries the narrative +
  design, not a copy of it. Promote any "why" beyond one sentence
  to a chores `###` subsection rather than expanding the intro.
- **Session-repo body**: same shape; bullets describe in-session
  activity rather than code changes.
- Examples:
  - `feat: add fix-ochid subcommand (0.22.0)`
  - `fix: fix-ochid prefix bug (0.22.1)`
  - `refactor: deduplicate common CLI flags (0.21.1)`

## Pre-commit Requirements

### User approval

Never execute commit, squash, push, or finalize commands without the
user's explicit approval. Present changes for review first; only run
them after the user confirms. This applies to late changes too —
pause for review before squashing into an existing commit.

### Review before proposing the commit block

After finishing a unit of work, **summarize what changed and stop
there**. Do not pre-emptively lay out the Checkpoint-1 commit
commands. Wait for the user to signal review is complete before
proposing the commit block. Changes during review are the norm,
not the exception; proposing commit text too early creates noise
and signals that I consider the work done when it usually isn't.

This applies per-step in a multi-step flow too — each step gets a
review pause before its commit block appears.

Signals that review is complete include explicit approval ("let's
commit", "looks good, commit it") **and any directive to start the
next step** ("do step 4", "next", "go N+1"). In that case the
previous step must be committed first — always commit the current
step before starting the next; don't ask.

### Per-file review checkpoints

The "review before commit block" rule applies to in-progress work
too, at finer grain. After each file edit, STOP, summarize what
changed, and wait for explicit go-ahead before touching the next
file or running follow-on commands (cargo test/install, dogfood
invocations, `vc-x1 …`, etc.).

**Exceptions** — both ride along with the change they accompany,
no separate review pause:

- **Refactors where code is moving across files** — e.g.
  lifting helpers into a new module and updating the original
  file's imports in the same change. Reviewing each half in
  isolation isn't useful.
- **`Cargo.toml` version bumps** that go with a specific code
  change.

**Why:** the user reviews diffs as work lands. Chaining multiple
file edits without pausing forces them to untangle cumulative
state instead of inspecting each step in isolation.

**How to apply:**

- "continue", "go", "do it", "lg" approves *the next unit
  only*, not all remaining units of a multi-file plan. A green
  light to proceed with a *direction* is not a green light to
  skip per-step checkpoints.
- After landing a unit: brief summary (2–5 lines) and stop. No
  cargo build / test / install / dogfood runs unless the user
  explicitly asks.
- In addition to (not replacement for) the
  Review-before-commit-block rule above.
- **Sub-step exception:** within a multi-step cycle's
  sub-step (or sub-sub-step) ladder, the per-step checkpoints
  defer to the commit-first review model — see
  [Sub-step Workflow > Commit-first review model](#commit-first-review-model).
  Sub-step commits land as the bot finishes them; user reviews
  the committed revision in their editor. The cycle-level
  push at close-out keeps the two-gate ceremony.

### Notes references

Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render
— `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]` for several (comma-separated, not
`[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)`
links stay single-bracketed. See
[Todo format](notes/README.md#todo-format) for details.

### Markdown anchor links

GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric
characters in place, map remaining spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do
**not** collapse adjacent whitespace — so `a + b` → `a--b` (spaces
on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` → `a-b` (only trailing space on
`:`). General markdown reference:
[markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub
publishes no official spec for auto-generated anchors; the
de-facto reference implementation is
[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).

### Versioning

Every plan must start with a version bump. Choose the approach based
on scope:

- **Single-step** (recommended for mechanical/focused changes): bump
  directly to `X.Y.Z`, implement in one commit. Simpler history.
- **Multi-step** (for exploratory/large changes): bump to `X.Y.Z-0`,
  implement across multiple commits incrementing the numeric
  suffix. The final commit drops the suffix.

The plan should recommend one approach and get user approval before
starting.

A plan that picks up a `## Todo` item — or *re-scopes* an
existing `## In Progress` ladder to absorb one — **deletes that
`## Todo` entry in the same commit** (the version-bump / plan
commit). `## In Progress` is the sole record of that work until
close-out, when it moves to `## Done`; a cycle that merges
several entangled `## Todo` items deletes all of them. A `## Todo`
entry that duplicates current `## In Progress` work is a process
bug.

For multi-step:

1. Bump version to `X.Y.Z-0` with the plan and commit as a chore
   marker.
2. Implement in one or more `X.Y.Z-N` commits (increment N as
   needed).
3. Final commit bumps to `X.Y.Z` (no suffix), updates
   `notes/todo.md` and `notes/chores-*.md` — this is the "done"
   marker.

Multi-step cycles surface the ladder at the top of
`notes/todo.md > ## In Progress` as a bullet list with `(done)` /
`(current)` markers — see the file's intro paragraph for the
format. When starting a new step, the *first* edit is to mark
that step `(current)` in `notes/todo.md` — before any code/doc
work — so the In Progress view reflects what's actually
happening. The flip back to `(done)` is part of the pre-commit
checklist (item 6).

**Why numeric suffixes (`-0`, `-1`, …) rather than `-devN`:**
semver pre-release identifiers may consist of a single numeric
component, and they compare numerically per spec. So
`X.Y.Z-1 < X.Y.Z-2 < … < X.Y.Z` correctly orders the dev ladder
below the done marker. Cargo accepts this form. The `-dev` prefix
adds no information the git log doesn't already convey and
doubles typing per commit.

The final release commit (no suffix) signals completion rather than
amending prior commits. This keeps history readable and makes it easy
to see which commits were exploratory vs final.

For decomposition finer than `X.Y.Z-N` — sub-steps (`X.Y.Z-N.M`)
or sub-sub-steps (`X.Y.Z-N.M-K`) — see
[Sub-step Workflow](#sub-step-workflow). The cycle close-out
choice (squash to one commit vs land each sub-step separately)
is made at close-out, not cycle start.

See also [`notes/substep-protocol.md`](notes/substep-protocol.md)
for the full protocol — when to use, per-substep contract
(`cargo test --bins` is non-negotiable), navigation, the validated
close-out squash recipe, and recovery. Revset primitives the
protocol relies on (`@`, `@-`, `..`, `::`, prefix matching) live in
[`notes/jj-revsets.md`](notes/jj-revsets.md).

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A `chores-NN.md` `##` section header that records a specific
commit, the matching `todo.md > ## Done` entry, and any `[N]`
reference to that section all use **exactly that commit's
title** — `<type>: <desc> (<version>)`, the same string the
commit gets (see [Commit Message Style](#commit-message-style)).
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: port push to Context
(0.48.0-6)` and the Done line `- refactor: port push to Context
(0.48.0-6) [[3]]`. For a multi-step cycle the `## Done` entry
uses the close-out commit's title.

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`,
`## In Progress`, `# References`) or to design `###` subsections
inside a chores section — those are named for whatever fits.
Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong
default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to
line a record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in
progress; the *last* edit before `vc-x1 push` syncs it — and the
`## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit — to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links)
for the slug algorithm; the pre-commit checklist catches a
dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should too
(and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Existing sections and `## Done` entries (most of chores-01..09;
the pre-`0.48.1` `## Done` lines) predate this and keep their
free-form text; the convention applies going forward — `0.48.2`
converts the `0.48.1` section + its Done entry as the worked
example.

### Chores section content — no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: a `Commits:` line (first line under the
header — see below), then [Prose form](#prose-form) (intro +
bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###` design
subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** — design points,
structural notes — never a per-file edit list. That lives in the
commit message body, which is the source of truth for "what
changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally
scoped to the commit). The chores section is the source of truth
for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither restates the
other.

When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism,
hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it — promote that to its
own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the
wrinkle is a live design concern (something that *should*
change, not just be recorded), also add a `notes/todo.md` item
with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo→chores is the
normal ref direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified
to be the same content in two places — and detail written twice
drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
narrative; `Commits:` links them.

### Chores commit references

The first line under a chores section header is a `Commits:`
line citing the git commit(s) that section records:

```
## refactor: port push to Context (0.48.0-6)

Commits: [[3]]

<intro paragraph...>
```

`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
[notes/README.md](notes/README.md#reference-numbering)),
**double-bracketed** so the brackets render — `Commits: [[3]]`,
or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a
literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner
`[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition — CommonMark /
GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition
puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub /
  GitLab resolve a unique prefix to the canonical commit page
  (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous —
  it survives a repo host change, `git show <40-hex>` works in
  any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a
  database, say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** The commit doesn't exist when its chores section is
written, so the `Commits:` line is **backfilled when the next
change to that repo is started** — the cycle-start step grabs
the just-pushed commit's URL + SHA and fills it in. The single
newest section is briefly `Commits:`-less; that's fine — the
commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "(X.Y.Z)"`
finds it.

### Pre-commit checklist

At cycle *start* (before the version bump): (a) backfill the
previous chores section's `Commits:` ref with the just-pushed
commit's URL + full SHA — see
[Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references); (b) if
this cycle picks up a `## Todo` item (or re-scopes `## In
Progress` to absorb one), delete that `## Todo` entry — see
[Versioning](#versioning).

Before proposing a commit, run all of the following and fix any issues:

1. `cargo fmt`
2. `cargo clippy`
3. `cargo test`
4. `cargo install --path . --locked` (if applicable) — `--locked`
   is required: without it, `cargo install` ignores `Cargo.lock`
   and re-resolves from scratch, which can pick incompatible
   versions even when `cargo build` / `cargo test` succeed.
5. Retest after install
6. Update `notes/todo.md` — for multi-step cycles, flip the
   just-completed step's marker from `(current)` to `(done)`
   **before** running `vc-x1 push`. The commit being pushed
   should reflect the new state. (The next step's `(current)`
   marker is set later, at the *start* of that step — see the
   Versioning multi-step section.)
7. Update `notes/todo.md` — at cycle close-out (final commit),
   move the entry from `## In Progress` to `## Done`.
8. Update `notes/chores-*.md` — add a section (header =
   provisional commit title; intro paragraph + any `###` design
   subsections; **no** per-file edit list — that's the commit
   body).
9. Sync the chores section header to the **final** commit title
   and update every markdown anchor back-reference to it.
10. Update `notes/README.md` — if functionality changed (new
    flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

## Sub-step Workflow

Larger work decomposes into named depths. The version-suffix
scheme nests:

- **Single step** — one change, one commit + push + finalize.
- **Multi-step** — planned series within a target bump:
  `0.5.0 → 0.6.0-0`, `0.6.0-0 → 0.6.0-1`, …, `0.6.0-N → 0.6.0`.
- **Sub-step** — finer granularity within a step:
  `0.6.0-3.1 → 0.6.0-3.2 → … → 0.6.0-3` (close-out).
- **Sub-sub-step** — finer still:
  `0.6.0-3.4-0 → 0.6.0-3.4-1 → … → 0.6.0-3.4` (close-out).

The conventions below apply at **whichever leaf depth the
current cycle planned to** — sub-step, sub-sub-step, etc.
"Sub-step" reads as shorthand for that leaf level throughout
this section.

### Version suffix in titles and Cargo.toml

Sub-step commits carry the leaf-level version in commit titles
**and** `Cargo.toml`. So `vc-x1 -V` shows the active sub-step
at build time. Bump Cargo.toml at the start of each sub-step
(extends the existing `X.Y.Z-N` step-start bump rule down a
level).

Cargo accepts arbitrary numeric segments in semver pre-release
identifiers; lexical comparison gives the expected ordering
(`0.6.0-3.4-1 < 0.6.0-3.4-2 < 0.6.0-3.4`).

### todo.md status flips

Markers in `notes/todo.md > ## In Progress` flip on a defined
cadence:

- **Start of (M):** mark (M) `(current)` as the first edit.
- **End of (M):** flip (M) `(current)` → `(done)` **before**
  the cargo cycle and commit. The commit captures the
  completed state.
- **Start of (M+1):** mark (M+1) `(current)` as that
  sub-step's first edit.

Each sub-step's commit carries the "this sub-step is done"
record; the next sub-step's commit carries "next sub-step
starts."

### Pre-commit cargo cycle (per sub-step)

Run before every sub-step commit (not just at cycle close-out):

1. `cargo fmt`
2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
3. `cargo test`
4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
5. (re-test if anything substantive)

Keeps every intermediate commit buildable so bisection works
across the cycle's stack.

### Commit-first review model

Per sub-step:

1. Make the sub-step changes.
2. Run the cargo cycle.
3. **Commit immediately** (both repos with ochid trailers, no
   separate approval gate at sub-step granularity).
4. Summarize the commit briefly in chat.
5. User reviews the committed revision in their editor (full
   file context, not chat-pasted diffs).
6. User iterates if needed; bot squashes follow-ups into the
   sub-step commit via `jj squash --into @-` (and
   `jj describe @-` — plus the chores section header and its
   anchor back-refs — if the title needs to change).
7. User signals "go to (M+1)" to advance.

This **replaces** the per-sub-step review pause that the
top-level `### Review before proposing the commit block` and
`### Per-file review checkpoints` rules would otherwise
impose. Local jj commits are mutable until close-out, so
committing freely is safe.

The two-gate ceremony (review + message approval) is preserved
for the **cycle-level push** at close-out — that crosses the
local→remote boundary and warrants explicit approval.

### Ochid trailers on sub-step commits

Sub-step commits include ochid trailers paired across the two
repos (same shape as top-level cycle commits):

- App body: `ochid: /.claude/<.claude-chid>`
- `.claude` body: `ochid: /<app-chid>`

Use `vc-x1 chid -s code,bot -L` to capture both pre-commit
change IDs (first line app, second `.claude`).

### `.claude` cadence

`.claude` commits **per sub-step alongside the app repo**.
Each sub-step's `.claude` commit captures the session state at
that moment.

Alternative considered (`.claude` accumulates across the cycle
and commits once at close-out) was rejected — keeping the
per-sub-step pairing preserves flexibility (any sub-step can
be promoted to its own push without restructuring).

**`.claude` is a linear journal — all session work lives on
`main`.** The repo has no need for parallel feature-branch
bookmarks to mirror app-side branches. When the app sits on
e.g. `init-clone-refactor`, `.claude` still commits to `main`.
Cross-references between sides are carried by the `ochid:`
trailer + commit timestamps; that's enough to associate
session activity with whichever app-side branch the cycle was
on.

**Do not create or maintain `.claude` bookmarks that mirror
app-side branches.** This was tried once during 0.41.1-6.7 on
the impression that an app-side fork needed a `.claude`
partner; the partner bookmark went unused for the cycle and
the work landed on `.claude main` regardless. Keeping such
bookmarks risks the bot misreading them as "this branch needs
to advance" and steering session pushes to the wrong remote
ref.

### Cycle close-out — squash or keep separate?

Two valid shapes for landing the sub-step stack on `main`:

- **Squash to one cycle commit** — single entry on `main`;
  sub-step granularity preserved only in the commit body's
  edit list. Right when the work is one logical change with
  intermediate validation points. **Cost:** the per-sub-step
  chores sections collapse into one, whose header becomes the
  single close-out commit title, and every anchor back-ref to a
  now-gone per-sub-step section gets re-pointed — real work,
  done as part of the squash.
- **Keep separate (N + 1 commits)** when the decomposition is
  itself informative (different conceptual stages, design
  progression worth showing in `git log`). Used on
  `0.41.1-6.7` (8 sub-sub-step commits + 1 close-out commit).
  Each section keeps its own header / `Commits:` ref — no
  consolidation churn.

Pick at close-out, not at cycle start. No firm default — weigh
the squash's chores-consolidation cost against a cleaner
`git log`; that cost biases toward keeping separate unless the
decomposition genuinely isn't informative.

### Reviewing committed sub-steps

The commit-first model assumes the reviewer can read the diff
of an already-committed revision. Don't `jj edit -r @-` back
into a past commit to view it — that marks the commit mutable,
shifts the WC pointer, forces a `jj new -r <head>` recovery.
Use one of:

**Terminal (always works):**

```
jj diff -r @-                  # diff of previous commit
jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>    # diff between two arbitrary revs
jj show -r <X>                 # description + diff for one rev
jj log -r @-..@                # what's between two points
```

Pipe through `delta` / `diff-so-fancy | less -R` for color and
side-by-side.

**External diff tool** — configure jj to launch your editor:

```
# ~/.config/jj/config.toml
[ui]
diff-editor = ["zed", "--diff", "$left", "$right"]
```

Then `jj diff -r @-` opens the configured tool. Works for
arbitrary `--from`/`--to` ranges.

**VS Code** — Source Control panel → Commit Graph →
right-click commit A → "Copy Commit ID" → right-click commit
B → "Compare with…" → paste / pick A. Two-commit diff opens
with the changed-files list. GitLens extension adds richer
"Open Comparison" actions; `Git: Compare with…` in the
Command Palette is a fallback.

## Code Conventions

### Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every
function and method must have a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief —
one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline is that the
comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments"
default that applies to inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the
module / item surface are expected; inline explanatory comments
inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive
`--help` output. Clap reflows by default and collapses bullets
into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- …` lands on
its own line in the rendered help.

### `// OK: …` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

Non-test code that calls `.unwrap()`, `.unwrap_or(…)`,
`.unwrap_or_default()`, or `.unwrap_or_else(…)` must have a trailing
`// OK: …` comment that justifies why the call is acceptable.

- `// OK: <specific reason>` — document the real precondition,
  invariant, or domain reason. Preferred whenever the reason isn't
  self-evident.
- `// OK: obvious` — the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
  `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")` — empty desc → empty title).

Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment).
Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are not used because they require a decoder
ring for readers seeing the code out of context.

For provably-unreachable `.unwrap()` calls, also prefix with
`#[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]` so the site stays silent if we enable
the project-wide `clippy::unwrap_used` lint later.

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt — panicking on setup failure is the
correct test behavior.

### Ask for clarification on ambiguous input

When user input is ambiguous or missing necessary detail, stop and
ask a specific question. Do not proceed on a guess and hope the
result lands right — a clarifying question costs a few seconds;
redoing misaligned work costs much more.

### Recognize when stuck

If a simple task has eaten 5+ minutes of thinking or back-and-forth
without progress, stop. Summarize what's blocking — unclear
requirements, unfamiliar API surface, conflicting signals — and ask.
Continued flailing produces worse outcomes than a direct "I'm stuck
on X."

## ochid Trailers

Every commit body must include an `ochid:` trailer pointing to the
counterpart commit in the other repo. The value is a workspace-root-relative
path followed by the changeID:

- App repo commits point to `.claude`: `ochid: /.claude/<changeID>`
- Bot session commits point to app repo: `ochid: /<changeID>`

Use `vc-x1 chid -s code,bot -L` to get both changeIDs (first line
is app repo, second is `.claude`).

## Commit-Push-Finalize Flow

**Use `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` — it wraps the full flow in one
command with two interactive approval gates.** Push runs
preflight (sync + fmt + clippy + test), prompts for review,
composes the commit message (via `--title`/`--body` or `$EDITOR`),
prompts for message approval, then commits both repos → advances
bookmarks → pushes app → finalizes `.claude`. Failures inside the
local mutation window roll both repos back via `jj op restore`;
after `push-app` succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

**Run this flow after every step** — not only at session end.
Single-step and multi-step changes are of equal importance: a
single-step change is one `push` invocation; a multi-step change
is one `push` per `X.Y.Z-N` commit plus one for the final release
commit. Each step gets its own commit, its own push, and its own
finalize — so dev markers land on the remote and in `.claude` as
they happen rather than being batched until the end.

### Run `vc-x1 push`

`<bookmark>` below is the **app-side working branch** — the
bookmark sitting at the tip of the chain `vc-x1 push` should
advance and push. For most cycles this is `main`; for
feature-branch work it's the feature-branch name (e.g.
`init-clone-refactor`). Pass the literal name, not the
placeholder. **`.claude` always pushes its `main`** regardless
of the app-side bookmark passed (see
[`.claude` cadence](#claude-cadence) — `.claude` is a linear
journal).

```
vc-x1 push <bookmark>                                  # interactive (review + $EDITOR)
vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."       # flags skip $EDITOR
vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..." # full non-interactive
vc-x1 push <bookmark> --dry-run                        # preview (no side effects)
vc-x1 push <bookmark> --from commit-app                # resume from specific stage
vc-x1 push --status                                    # show saved state
vc-x1 push <bookmark> --restart                        # clear saved state; start fresh
```

**Bookmark mismatch is currently silent.** `vc-x1 push`
doesn't verify that `<bookmark>` matches the working-copy
chain — passing a bookmark whose tip isn't an ancestor of `@`
will (silently) push that bookmark anyway, leaving your work
unpushed. Always confirm `jj log -r <bookmark>..@` shows the
commits you mean to send. A safety check is on the 0.42.0
todo (`vc-x1 push: --scope` flag item).

The two approval gates are surfaced by push itself:

1. **Review** — push prints `jj diff --stat` for both repos and
   prompts `[y/N]`. Approve = "the work is done right".
2. **Message** — push either uses `--title`/`--body` (non-editor
   path) or opens `$EDITOR` on a template. Approve = "the message
   reads right".

Both titles and bodies are the **same** across the two commits;
only the `ochid:` trailer differs per repo. Push collects the
pre-commit chids internally so you don't hand-manage them.

For the full flag list and stage machine, see `vc-x1 push --help`
and `notes/chores-05.md > Add push subcommand (0.37.0)`.

### Bot communication during the flow

When applying the flow on the user's behalf, use plain prose at
each gate — no insider jargon ("Gate N signal", "Checkpoint N",
etc.):

1. **After completing the work** — summarize what changed
   (file-by-file or feature-by-feature, terse) and end with
   something like:

   > Work complete. Please review. On approval I'll prep the
   > commit title and body for a second approval before pushing.

2. **After review approval** — present the proposed `$TITLE` and
   `$BODY` explicitly, then ask permission to run `vc-x1 push`.
   Do **not** spell out the full
   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "$TITLE" --body "$BODY"`
   invocation by default — it's mechanical and obvious from the
   title/body. Show it only on explicit request (verbose mode /
   debugging).

3. **After execution approval** — run the push command. `push`
   handles commit + bookmark + push + finalize internally;
   nothing should be output after the push command (finalize is
   detached and absolute-last; see "After finalize: stop and
   wait" below).

### Pre-step: `vc-x1 sync` (still useful)

Push's preflight runs `vc-x1 sync --check` as its first step. Check
mode verifies divergence without applying — if anything is `behind`
or `diverged`, preflight errors and you resolve explicitly with
`vc-x1 sync --no-check` before re-running push. This keeps the
two approval gates (review, message) authoritative; push never
performs an unsupervised rebase.

Running sync manually before you *start* editing is still cheap
(one line when clean) and surfaces remote changes earlier:

```
vc-x1 sync --check                    # dual-repo workspace, verify
vc-x1 sync --no-check                 # apply (rebase / fast-forward)
vc-x1 sync --check -R .               # single-repo project
vc-x1 sync --check --quiet            # silent; exit code signals result
```

Bots and scripts must pass `--check` or `--no-check` explicitly —
defaults can shift, explicit flags lock in the contract. Interactive
use can take the default (which is `--check`).

Output shape:

- **Clean**: one line — `sync: N repos, all bookmarks up-to-date`.
  Note: scope is bookmark-vs-remote tracking, not working-copy
  cleanliness — `@` may have uncommitted changes; sync doesn't
  speak to that. Proceed.
- **Action needed** (`behind` / `diverged`) under `--check`:
  per-repo fetch + state lines, then a fatal
  `sync: N repos need action — resolve with vc-x1 sync --no-check
  and re-run`. Inspect, run `vc-x1 sync --no-check`, then proceed.
- **`--quiet`**: no output; exit code is the only signal.

### After finalize: stop and wait

After `vc-x1 finalize` is launched — **whether mid-session per-step
or at session end** — you **MUST NEVER** proceed to a next step, edit
files, run tools, or emit any text (prose, recaps, acknowledgements),
until the user explicitly directs you to continue. Treat finalize as
a hard stop for the whole turn. Any final words (e.g. "next is ...")
must be said in the approval prompt *before* executing finalize; the
finalize `Bash` call is the last thing in the turn and nothing
follows it.

This holds even when the next step seems obvious (e.g. "next is
N+1" or "now I should bump the version and commit the release").
Wait. The user controls cadence — every push+finalize is a checkpoint
they may want to inspect, think about, hand off, or take a break at.
Auto-proceeding bypasses that checkpoint and produces unwanted writes
between finalize and the next explicit instruction.

Exceptions to this rule may emerge later but are not authorized at
this stage. Until told otherwise, treat as absolute.

### Late changes after push

If the app repo needs a tweak after `push-app` succeeded (e.g.
updating CLAUDE.md or memory), the commit is immutable. Use
`--ignore-immutable` to squash the changes into `@-` — the
bookmark moves with the rewritten commit — then re-push:

```
jj squash --ignore-immutable -R .
jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .
```

If you squash somewhere other than `@-`, add
`jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <target> -R .` between those
two commands so the bookmark lands on the rewritten commit.

`.claude` is also mutable via this pattern when needed, though
push's `finalize-claude` stage normally handles trailing session
writes so you rarely hit this case there.

### Manual finalize fallback

If push exited before `finalize-claude` (e.g. `--no-finalize`
was set, or a failure between `push-app` and `finalize-claude`),
run finalize by hand:

```
vc-x1 finalize --repo .claude --squash --push <bookmark> --delay 10 --detach --log /tmp/vc-x1-finalize.log
```

**Nothing should happen after finalize** — no memory writes, no
tool calls, no additional output. If any work is done after
finalize, run finalize again so the trailing writes are captured.
Do **not** echo or restate the finalize output — the Bash tool
already displays it.

**Clear push's saved state after any out-of-band recovery** —
manual `vc-x1 finalize`, manual `jj squash --ignore-immutable`
+ force-push, etc., all leave `.vc-x1/push-state.toml` pointing
at a now-stale halt point. Either `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml`
or run `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --restart` (which clears and
restarts in one go) before the next `vc-x1 push`. Otherwise
push resumes from a bogus stage and can falsely declare
success.

35	Do not use the bot's per-project memory directory
36	(`~/.bot/projects/<path>/memory/`). In a dual-repo setup with

38	and it loses on discoverability:
39	
40	- **CLAUDE.md** — at the repo root, a well-known location for bot
41	  instructions, committed, reviewable, visible to every collaborator
42	  (human or bot).
43	- **Memory directory** — hidden under the user's home, tied to one
44	  machine, invisible to anyone but the bot, never diffed or reviewed.

49	## Speculation marker
50	
51	Durable text the bot writes — CLAUDE.md, `notes/`, commit bodies,
52	chores sections — should stick to observations and direct descriptions
53	of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal claim
54	enters the text, prefix it with "The bot thinks ..." so a reader can
55	tell the measured from the inferred.
56	
57	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader
58	(or the bot on a later session) can pick it up as a known fact when
59	it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction worth keeping visible
60	in the written record.
61	
62	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no
63	marker. Prefix with "The bot thinks ..." (or a close variant like
64	"The bot's guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins
65	because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal
66	state"), a prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any
67	reasoning not directly supported by the data on hand.

109	
110	Long-lived prose on this project follows one shape: a short intro
111	that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet
112	list for the details. Wrap lines at ≤72 cols (bullet continuations
113	indent two spaces). Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs — they hide the
114	structure that bullets make scannable.

116	Surfaces that use this shape:

118	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files —

121	  ≤50-col title is the commit-specific add-on; see

123	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores-NN.md` — see
124	  [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
125	- Todo and Done entries in `notes/todo.md` when an entry needs more

134	- **Chores / todo / done** — bullets are conceptual (design points,

141	## Commit Message Style
142	
143	Use [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) with
144	a version suffix:
145	
146	```
147	<type>: <short description> (<version>)
148	```
149	
150	- **Title**: ≤50 chars (the "50" of the git 50/72 rule), a short
151	  summary of *what* changed. The version suffix counts toward the
152	  50 — the descriptive part gets whatever's left after `<type>: `
153	  and ` (<version>)`, so favor terse phrasings (`port X to Context`
154	  over `X → Context + XParams`) when the names run long. Common
155	  types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`.
156	- **Body**: [Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets), wrap
157	  ≤72 (the "72" of the 50/72 rule). App-repo bullets are
158	  **file-by-file** — one bullet per file changed, file plus a
159	  one-line gist. This list **is the source of truth** for the
160	  cycle's mechanical change record; chores carries the narrative +
161	  design, not a copy of it. Promote any "why" beyond one sentence
162	  to a chores `###` subsection rather than expanding the intro.
163	- **Session-repo body**: same shape; bullets describe in-session
164	  activity rather than code changes.
165	- Examples:
166	  - `feat: add fix-ochid subcommand (0.22.0)`
167	  - `fix: fix-ochid prefix bug (0.22.1)`
168	  - `refactor: deduplicate common CLI flags (0.21.1)`

170	## Pre-commit Requirements
171	
172	### User approval
173	
174	Never execute commit, squash, push, or finalize commands without the
175	user's explicit approval. Present changes for review first; only run
176	them after the user confirms. This applies to late changes too —
177	pause for review before squashing into an existing commit.
178	
179	### Review before proposing the commit block
180	
181	After finishing a unit of work, **summarize what changed and stop
182	there**. Do not pre-emptively lay out the Checkpoint-1 commit
183	commands. Wait for the user to signal review is complete before
184	proposing the commit block. Changes during review are the norm,
185	not the exception; proposing commit text too early creates noise
186	and signals that I consider the work done when it usually isn't.
187	
188	This applies per-step in a multi-step flow too — each step gets a
189	review pause before its commit block appears.
190	
191	Signals that review is complete include explicit approval ("let's
192	commit", "looks good, commit it") **and any directive to start the
193	next step** ("do step 4", "next", "go N+1"). In that case the
194	previous step must be committed first — always commit the current
195	step before starting the next; don't ask.
196	
197	### Per-file review checkpoints
198	
199	The "review before commit block" rule applies to in-progress work
200	too, at finer grain. After each file edit, STOP, summarize what
201	changed, and wait for explicit go-ahead before touching the next
202	file or running follow-on commands (cargo test/install, dogfood
203	invocations, `vc-x1 …`, etc.).
204	
205	**Exceptions** — both ride along with the change they accompany,
206	no separate review pause:
207	
208	- **Refactors where code is moving across files** — e.g.
209	  lifting helpers into a new module and updating the original
210	  file's imports in the same change. Reviewing each half in
211	  isolation isn't useful.
212	- **`Cargo.toml` version bumps** that go with a specific code
213	  change.
214	
215	**Why:** the user reviews diffs as work lands. Chaining multiple
216	file edits without pausing forces them to untangle cumulative
217	state instead of inspecting each step in isolation.
218	
219	**How to apply:**
220	
221	- "continue", "go", "do it", "lg" approves *the next unit
222	  only*, not all remaining units of a multi-file plan. A green
223	  light to proceed with a *direction* is not a green light to
224	  skip per-step checkpoints.
225	- After landing a unit: brief summary (2–5 lines) and stop. No
226	  cargo build / test / install / dogfood runs unless the user
227	  explicitly asks.
228	- In addition to (not replacement for) the
229	  Review-before-commit-block rule above.
230	- **Sub-step exception:** within a multi-step cycle's
231	  sub-step (or sub-sub-step) ladder, the per-step checkpoints
232	  defer to the commit-first review model — see
233	  [Sub-step Workflow > Commit-first review model](#commit-first-review-model).
234	  Sub-step commits land as the bot finishes them; user reviews
235	  the committed revision in their editor. The cycle-level
236	  push at close-out keeps the two-gate ceremony.
237	
238	### Notes references
239	
240	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render
241	— `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]` for several (comma-separated, not
242	`[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
243	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)`
244	links stay single-bracketed. See
245	[Todo format](notes/README.md#todo-format) for details.

247	### Markdown anchor links
248	
249	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric
250	characters in place, map remaining spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do
251	**not** collapse adjacent whitespace — so `a + b` → `a--b` (spaces
252	on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` → `a-b` (only trailing space on
253	`:`). General markdown reference:
254	[markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub
255	publishes no official spec for auto-generated anchors; the
256	de-facto reference implementation is
257	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
258	
259	### Versioning
260	
261	Every plan must start with a version bump. Choose the approach based
262	on scope:
263	
264	- **Single-step** (recommended for mechanical/focused changes): bump
265	  directly to `X.Y.Z`, implement in one commit. Simpler history.
266	- **Multi-step** (for exploratory/large changes): bump to `X.Y.Z-0`,
267	  implement across multiple commits incrementing the numeric
268	  suffix. The final commit drops the suffix.
269	
270	The plan should recommend one approach and get user approval before
271	starting.
272	
273	A plan that picks up a `## Todo` item — or *re-scopes* an
274	existing `## In Progress` ladder to absorb one — **deletes that
275	`## Todo` entry in the same commit** (the version-bump / plan
276	commit). `## In Progress` is the sole record of that work until
277	close-out, when it moves to `## Done`; a cycle that merges
278	several entangled `## Todo` items deletes all of them. A `## Todo`
279	entry that duplicates current `## In Progress` work is a process
280	bug.
281	
282	For multi-step:
283	
284	1. Bump version to `X.Y.Z-0` with the plan and commit as a chore
285	   marker.
286	2. Implement in one or more `X.Y.Z-N` commits (increment N as
287	   needed).
288	3. Final commit bumps to `X.Y.Z` (no suffix), updates
289	   `notes/todo.md` and `notes/chores-*.md` — this is the "done"
290	   marker.
291	
292	Multi-step cycles surface the ladder at the top of
293	`notes/todo.md > ## In Progress` as a bullet list with `(done)` /
294	`(current)` markers — see the file's intro paragraph for the
295	format. When starting a new step, the *first* edit is to mark
296	that step `(current)` in `notes/todo.md` — before any code/doc
297	work — so the In Progress view reflects what's actually
298	happening. The flip back to `(done)` is part of the pre-commit
299	checklist (item 6).
300	
301	**Why numeric suffixes (`-0`, `-1`, …) rather than `-devN`:**
302	semver pre-release identifiers may consist of a single numeric
303	component, and they compare numerically per spec. So
304	`X.Y.Z-1 < X.Y.Z-2 < … < X.Y.Z` correctly orders the dev ladder
305	below the done marker. Cargo accepts this form. The `-dev` prefix
306	adds no information the git log doesn't already convey and
307	doubles typing per commit.
308	
309	The final release commit (no suffix) signals completion rather than
310	amending prior commits. This keeps history readable and makes it easy
311	to see which commits were exploratory vs final.
312	
313	For decomposition finer than `X.Y.Z-N` — sub-steps (`X.Y.Z-N.M`)
314	or sub-sub-steps (`X.Y.Z-N.M-K`) — see
315	[Sub-step Workflow](#sub-step-workflow). The cycle close-out
316	choice (squash to one commit vs land each sub-step separately)
317	is made at close-out, not cycle start.
318	
319	See also [`notes/substep-protocol.md`](notes/substep-protocol.md)
320	for the full protocol — when to use, per-substep contract
321	(`cargo test --bins` is non-negotiable), navigation, the validated
322	close-out squash recipe, and recovery. Revset primitives the
323	protocol relies on (`@`, `@-`, `..`, `::`, prefix matching) live in
324	[`notes/jj-revsets.md`](notes/jj-revsets.md).
325	
326	### Headings and entries that record a commit
327	
328	A `chores-NN.md` `##` section header that records a specific
329	commit, the matching `todo.md > ## Done` entry, and any `[N]`
330	reference to that section all use **exactly that commit's
331	title** — `<type>: <desc> (<version>)`, the same string the
332	commit gets (see [Commit Message Style](#commit-message-style)).
333	E.g. the chores header `## refactor: port push to Context
334	(0.48.0-6)` and the Done line `- refactor: port push to Context
335	(0.48.0-6) [[3]]`. For a multi-step cycle the `## Done` entry
336	uses the close-out commit's title.
337	
338	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`,
339	`## In Progress`, `# References`) or to design `###` subsections
340	inside a chores section — those are named for whatever fits.
341	Among the commit-recording ones, exact match is the strong
342	default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to
343	line a record up with its commit.
344	
345	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in
346	progress; the *last* edit before `vc-x1 push` syncs it — and the
347	`## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit — to the final
348	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links)
349	for the slug algorithm; the pre-commit checklist catches a
350	dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should too
351	(and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
352	
353	Existing sections and `## Done` entries (most of chores-01..09;
354	the pre-`0.48.1` `## Done` lines) predate this and keep their
355	free-form text; the convention applies going forward — `0.48.2`
356	converts the `0.48.1` section + its Done entry as the worked
357	example.
358	
359	### Chores section content — no edit list; git is the record
360	
361	A chores section is: a `Commits:` line (first line under the
362	header — see below), then [Prose form](#prose-form) (intro +
363	bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###` design
364	subsections. Bullets here are **conceptual** — design points,
365	structural notes — never a per-file edit list. That lives in the
366	commit message body, which is the source of truth for "what
367	changed mechanically" (immutable, `git show`-able, naturally
368	scoped to the commit). The chores section is the source of truth
369	for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither restates the
370	other.
371	
372	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism,
373	hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it — promote that to its
374	own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the
375	wrinkle is a live design concern (something that *should*
376	change, not just be recorded), also add a `notes/todo.md` item
377	with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo→chores is the
378	normal ref direction).
379	
380	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified
381	to be the same content in two places — and detail written twice
382	drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the
383	narrative; `Commits:` links them.
384	
385	### Chores commit references
386	
387	The first line under a chores section header is a `Commits:`
388	line citing the git commit(s) that section records:
389	
390	```
391	## refactor: port push to Context (0.48.0-6)
392	
393	Commits: [[3]]
394	
395	<intro paragraph...>
396	```
397	
398	`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
399	[notes/README.md](notes/README.md#reference-numbering)),
400	**double-bracketed** so the brackets render — `Commits: [[3]]`,
401	or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a
402	literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner
403	`[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition — CommonMark /
404	GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition
405	puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
406	40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
407	
408	```
409	[3]: https://github.com/winksaville/vc-x1/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
410	```
411	
412	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub /
413	  GitLab resolve a unique prefix to the canonical commit page
414	  (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
415	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous —
416	  it survives a repo host change, `git show <40-hex>` works in
417	  any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a
418	  database, say) gets the canonical identifier.
419	
420	**Timing.** The commit doesn't exist when its chores section is
421	written, so the `Commits:` line is **backfilled when the next
422	change to that repo is started** — the cycle-start step grabs
423	the just-pushed commit's URL + SHA and fills it in. The single
424	newest section is briefly `Commits:`-less; that's fine — the
425	commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "(X.Y.Z)"`
426	finds it.
427	
428	### Pre-commit checklist
429	
430	At cycle *start* (before the version bump): (a) backfill the
431	previous chores section's `Commits:` ref with the just-pushed
432	commit's URL + full SHA — see
433	[Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references); (b) if
434	this cycle picks up a `## Todo` item (or re-scopes `## In
435	Progress` to absorb one), delete that `## Todo` entry — see
436	[Versioning](#versioning).
437	
438	Before proposing a commit, run all of the following and fix any issues:
439	
440	1. `cargo fmt`
441	2. `cargo clippy`
442	3. `cargo test`
443	4. `cargo install --path . --locked` (if applicable) — `--locked`
444	   is required: without it, `cargo install` ignores `Cargo.lock`
445	   and re-resolves from scratch, which can pick incompatible
446	   versions even when `cargo build` / `cargo test` succeed.
447	5. Retest after install
448	6. Update `notes/todo.md` — for multi-step cycles, flip the
449	   just-completed step's marker from `(current)` to `(done)`
450	   **before** running `vc-x1 push`. The commit being pushed

452	   marker is set later, at the *start* of that step — see the

454	7. Update `notes/todo.md` — at cycle close-out (final commit),
455	   move the entry from `## In Progress` to `## Done`.
456	8. Update `notes/chores-*.md` — add a section (header =
457	   provisional commit title; intro paragraph + any `###` design
458	   subsections; **no** per-file edit list — that's the commit
459	   body).
460	9. Sync the chores section header to the **final** commit title
461	   and update every markdown anchor back-reference to it.
462	10. Update `notes/README.md` — if functionality changed (new
463	    flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

465	## Sub-step Workflow
466	
467	Larger work decomposes into named depths. The version-suffix
468	scheme nests:
469	
470	- **Single step** — one change, one commit + push + finalize.
471	- **Multi-step** — planned series within a target bump:
472	  `0.5.0 → 0.6.0-0`, `0.6.0-0 → 0.6.0-1`, …, `0.6.0-N → 0.6.0`.
473	- **Sub-step** — finer granularity within a step:
474	  `0.6.0-3.1 → 0.6.0-3.2 → … → 0.6.0-3` (close-out).
475	- **Sub-sub-step** — finer still:
476	  `0.6.0-3.4-0 → 0.6.0-3.4-1 → … → 0.6.0-3.4` (close-out).
477	
478	The conventions below apply at **whichever leaf depth the
479	current cycle planned to** — sub-step, sub-sub-step, etc.
480	"Sub-step" reads as shorthand for that leaf level throughout
481	this section.
482	
483	### Version suffix in titles and Cargo.toml
484	
485	Sub-step commits carry the leaf-level version in commit titles
486	**and** `Cargo.toml`. So `vc-x1 -V` shows the active sub-step
487	at build time. Bump Cargo.toml at the start of each sub-step
488	(extends the existing `X.Y.Z-N` step-start bump rule down a
489	level).
490	
491	Cargo accepts arbitrary numeric segments in semver pre-release
492	identifiers; lexical comparison gives the expected ordering
493	(`0.6.0-3.4-1 < 0.6.0-3.4-2 < 0.6.0-3.4`).
494	
495	### todo.md status flips
496	
497	Markers in `notes/todo.md > ## In Progress` flip on a defined
498	cadence:
499	
500	- **Start of (M):** mark (M) `(current)` as the first edit.
501	- **End of (M):** flip (M) `(current)` → `(done)` **before**
502	  the cargo cycle and commit. The commit captures the
503	  completed state.
504	- **Start of (M+1):** mark (M+1) `(current)` as that
505	  sub-step's first edit.
506	
507	Each sub-step's commit carries the "this sub-step is done"
508	record; the next sub-step's commit carries "next sub-step
509	starts."
510	
511	### Pre-commit cargo cycle (per sub-step)
512	
513	Run before every sub-step commit (not just at cycle close-out):
514	
515	1. `cargo fmt`
516	2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
517	3. `cargo test`
518	4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
519	5. (re-test if anything substantive)
520	
521	Keeps every intermediate commit buildable so bisection works
522	across the cycle's stack.
523	
524	### Commit-first review model
525	
526	Per sub-step:
527	
528	1. Make the sub-step changes.
529	2. Run the cargo cycle.
530	3. **Commit immediately** (both repos with ochid trailers, no
531	   separate approval gate at sub-step granularity).
532	4. Summarize the commit briefly in chat.
533	5. User reviews the committed revision in their editor (full
534	   file context, not chat-pasted diffs).
535	6. User iterates if needed; bot squashes follow-ups into the
536	   sub-step commit via `jj squash --into @-` (and
537	   `jj describe @-` — plus the chores section header and its
538	   anchor back-refs — if the title needs to change).
539	7. User signals "go to (M+1)" to advance.
540	
541	This **replaces** the per-sub-step review pause that the
542	top-level `### Review before proposing the commit block` and
543	`### Per-file review checkpoints` rules would otherwise
544	impose. Local jj commits are mutable until close-out, so
545	committing freely is safe.
546	
547	The two-gate ceremony (review + message approval) is preserved
548	for the **cycle-level push** at close-out — that crosses the
549	local→remote boundary and warrants explicit approval.
550	
551	### Ochid trailers on sub-step commits
552	
553	Sub-step commits include ochid trailers paired across the two
554	repos (same shape as top-level cycle commits):
555	
556	- App body: `ochid: /.bot/<.bot-chid>`
557	- `.bot` body: `ochid: /<app-chid>`
558	
559	Use `vc-x1 chid -s code,bot -L` to capture both pre-commit
560	change IDs (first line app, second `.bot`).
561	
562	### `.bot` cadence
563	
564	`.bot` commits **per sub-step alongside the app repo**.
565	Each sub-step's `.bot` commit captures the session state at
566	that moment.
567	
568	Alternative considered (`.bot` accumulates across the cycle
569	and commits once at close-out) was rejected — keeping the
570	per-sub-step pairing preserves flexibility (any sub-step can
571	be promoted to its own push without restructuring).
572	
573	**`.bot` is a linear journal — all session work lives on
574	`main`.** The repo has no need for parallel feature-branch
575	bookmarks to mirror app-side branches. When the app sits on
576	e.g. `init-clone-refactor`, `.bot` still commits to `main`.
577	Cross-references between sides are carried by the `ochid:`
578	trailer + commit timestamps; that's enough to associate
579	session activity with whichever app-side branch the cycle was
580	on.
581	
582	**Do not create or maintain `.bot` bookmarks that mirror
583	app-side branches.** This was tried once during 0.41.1-6.7 on
584	the impression that an app-side fork needed a `.bot`
585	partner; the partner bookmark went unused for the cycle and
586	the work landed on `.bot main` regardless. Keeping such
587	bookmarks risks the bot misreading them as "this branch needs
588	to advance" and steering session pushes to the wrong remote
589	ref.
590	
591	### Cycle close-out — squash or keep separate?
592	
593	Two valid shapes for landing the sub-step stack on `main`:
594	
595	- **Squash to one cycle commit** — single entry on `main`;
596	  sub-step granularity preserved only in the commit body's
597	  edit list. Right when the work is one logical change with
598	  intermediate validation points. **Cost:** the per-sub-step
599	  chores sections collapse into one, whose header becomes the
600	  single close-out commit title, and every anchor back-ref to a
601	  now-gone per-sub-step section gets re-pointed — real work,
602	  done as part of the squash.
603	- **Keep separate (N + 1 commits)** when the decomposition is
604	  itself informative (different conceptual stages, design
605	  progression worth showing in `git log`). Used on
606	  `0.41.1-6.7` (8 sub-sub-step commits + 1 close-out commit).
607	  Each section keeps its own header / `Commits:` ref — no
608	  consolidation churn.
609	
610	Pick at close-out, not at cycle start. No firm default — weigh
611	the squash's chores-consolidation cost against a cleaner
612	`git log`; that cost biases toward keeping separate unless the
613	decomposition genuinely isn't informative.
614	
615	### Reviewing committed sub-steps
616	
617	The commit-first model assumes the reviewer can read the diff
618	of an already-committed revision. Don't `jj edit -r @-` back
619	into a past commit to view it — that marks the commit mutable,
620	shifts the WC pointer, forces a `jj new -r <head>` recovery.
621	Use one of:
622	
623	**Terminal (always works):**
624	
625	```
626	jj diff -r @-                  # diff of previous commit
627	jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>    # diff between two arbitrary revs
628	jj show -r <X>                 # description + diff for one rev
629	jj log -r @-..@                # what's between two points
630	```
631	
632	Pipe through `delta` / `diff-so-fancy | less -R` for color and
633	side-by-side.
634	
635	**External diff tool** — configure jj to launch your editor:
636	
637	```
638	# ~/.config/jj/config.toml
639	[ui]
640	diff-editor = ["zed", "--diff", "$left", "$right"]
641	```
642	
643	Then `jj diff -r @-` opens the configured tool. Works for
644	arbitrary `--from`/`--to` ranges.
645	
646	**VS Code** — Source Control panel → Commit Graph →
647	right-click commit A → "Copy Commit ID" → right-click commit
648	B → "Compare with…" → paste / pick A. Two-commit diff opens
649	with the changed-files list. GitLens extension adds richer
650	"Open Comparison" actions; `Git: Compare with…` in the
651	Command Palette is a fallback.
652	
653	## Code Conventions
654	
655	### Doc comments on every file, function, and method
656	
657	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every
658	function and method must have a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief —
659	one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline is that the
660	comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
661	[Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
662	
663	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments"
664	default that applies to inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the
665	module / item surface are expected; inline explanatory comments
666	inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
667	non-obvious WHY.
668	
669	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive
670	`--help` output. Clap reflows by default and collapses bullets
671	into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
672	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- …` lands on
673	its own line in the rendered help.
674	
675	### `// OK: …` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
676	
677	Non-test code that calls `.unwrap()`, `.unwrap_or(…)`,
678	`.unwrap_or_default()`, or `.unwrap_or_else(…)` must have a trailing
679	`// OK: …` comment that justifies why the call is acceptable.
680	
681	- `// OK: <specific reason>` — document the real precondition,
682	  invariant, or domain reason. Preferred whenever the reason isn't
683	  self-evident.
684	- `// OK: obvious` — the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
685	  `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")` — empty desc → empty title).
686	
687	Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment).
688	Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are not used because they require a decoder
689	ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
690	
691	For provably-unreachable `.unwrap()` calls, also prefix with
692	`#[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]` so the site stays silent if we enable
693	the project-wide `clippy::unwrap_used` lint later.
694	
695	```rust
696	let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
697	let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious
698	
699	match matches.len() {
700	    1 => {
701	        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
702	        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
703	        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
704	    }
705	    // ...
706	}
707	```
708	
709	Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt — panicking on setup failure is the
710	correct test behavior.
711	
712	### Ask for clarification on ambiguous input
713	
714	When user input is ambiguous or missing necessary detail, stop and
715	ask a specific question. Do not proceed on a guess and hope the
716	result lands right — a clarifying question costs a few seconds;
717	redoing misaligned work costs much more.
718	
719	### Recognize when stuck
720	
721	If a simple task has eaten 5+ minutes of thinking or back-and-forth
722	without progress, stop. Summarize what's blocking — unclear
723	requirements, unfamiliar API surface, conflicting signals — and ask.
724	Continued flailing produces worse outcomes than a direct "I'm stuck
725	on X."
726	
727	## ochid Trailers
728	
729	Every commit body must include an `ochid:` trailer pointing to the
730	counterpart commit in the other repo. The value is a workspace-root-relative
731	path followed by the changeID:
732	
733	- App repo commits point to `.bot`: `ochid: /.bot/<changeID>`
734	- Bot session commits point to app repo: `ochid: /<changeID>`
735	
736	Use `vc-x1 chid -s code,bot -L` to get both changeIDs (first line
737	is app repo, second is `.bot`).
738	
739	## Commit-Push-Finalize Flow
740	
741	**Use `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` — it wraps the full flow in one
742	command with two interactive approval gates.** Push runs
743	preflight (sync + fmt + clippy + test), prompts for review,
744	composes the commit message (via `--title`/`--body` or `$EDITOR`),
745	prompts for message approval, then commits both repos → advances
746	bookmarks → pushes app → finalizes `.bot`. Failures inside the
747	local mutation window roll both repos back via `jj op restore`;
748	after `push-app` succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
749	recovery is forward-only.
750	
751	**Run this flow after every step** — not only at session end.
752	Single-step and multi-step changes are of equal importance: a
753	single-step change is one `push` invocation; a multi-step change
754	is one `push` per `X.Y.Z-N` commit plus one for the final release
755	commit. Each step gets its own commit, its own push, and its own
756	finalize — so dev markers land on the remote and in `.bot` as
757	they happen rather than being batched until the end.
758	
759	### Run `vc-x1 push`
760	
761	`<bookmark>` below is the **app-side working branch** — the
762	bookmark sitting at the tip of the chain `vc-x1 push` should
763	advance and push. For most cycles this is `main`; for
764	feature-branch work it's the feature-branch name (e.g.
765	`init-clone-refactor`). Pass the literal name, not the
766	placeholder. **`.bot` always pushes its `main`** regardless
767	of the app-side bookmark passed (see
768	[`.bot` cadence](#claude-cadence) — `.bot` is a linear
769	journal).
770	
771	```
772	vc-x1 push <bookmark>                                  # interactive (review + $EDITOR)
773	vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."       # flags skip $EDITOR
774	vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "..." --body "..." # full non-interactive
775	vc-x1 push <bookmark> --dry-run                        # preview (no side effects)
776	vc-x1 push <bookmark> --from commit-app                # resume from specific stage
777	vc-x1 push --status                                    # show saved state
778	vc-x1 push <bookmark> --restart                        # clear saved state; start fresh
779	```
780	
781	**Bookmark mismatch is currently silent.** `vc-x1 push`
782	doesn't verify that `<bookmark>` matches the working-copy
783	chain — passing a bookmark whose tip isn't an ancestor of `@`
784	will (silently) push that bookmark anyway, leaving your work
785	unpushed. Always confirm `jj log -r <bookmark>..@` shows the
786	commits you mean to send. A safety check is on the 0.42.0
787	todo (`vc-x1 push: --scope` flag item).
788	
789	The two approval gates are surfaced by push itself:
790	
791	1. **Review** — push prints `jj diff --stat` for both repos and
792	   prompts `[y/N]`. Approve = "the work is done right".
793	2. **Message** — push either uses `--title`/`--body` (non-editor
794	   path) or opens `$EDITOR` on a template. Approve = "the message
795	   reads right".
796	
797	Both titles and bodies are the **same** across the two commits;
798	only the `ochid:` trailer differs per repo. Push collects the
799	pre-commit chids internally so you don't hand-manage them.
800	
801	For the full flag list and stage machine, see `vc-x1 push --help`
802	and `notes/chores-05.md > Add push subcommand (0.37.0)`.
803	
804	### Bot communication during the flow
805	
806	When applying the flow on the user's behalf, use plain prose at
807	each gate — no insider jargon ("Gate N signal", "Checkpoint N",
808	etc.):
809	
810	1. **After completing the work** — summarize what changed
811	   (file-by-file or feature-by-feature, terse) and end with
812	   something like:
813	
814	   > Work complete. Please review. On approval I'll prep the
815	   > commit title and body for a second approval before pushing.
816	
817	2. **After review approval** — present the proposed `$TITLE` and
818	   `$BODY` explicitly, then ask permission to run `vc-x1 push`.
819	   Do **not** spell out the full
820	   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --yes --title "$TITLE" --body "$BODY"`
821	   invocation by default — it's mechanical and obvious from the
822	   title/body. Show it only on explicit request (verbose mode /
823	   debugging).
824	
825	3. **After execution approval** — run the push command. `push`
826	   handles commit + bookmark + push + finalize internally;
827	   nothing should be output after the push command (finalize is
828	   detached and absolute-last; see "After finalize: stop and
829	   wait" below).
830	
831	### Pre-step: `vc-x1 sync` (still useful)
832	
833	Push's preflight runs `vc-x1 sync --check` as its first step. Check
834	mode verifies divergence without applying — if anything is `behind`
835	or `diverged`, preflight errors and you resolve explicitly with
836	`vc-x1 sync --no-check` before re-running push. This keeps the
837	two approval gates (review, message) authoritative; push never
838	performs an unsupervised rebase.
839	
840	Running sync manually before you *start* editing is still cheap
841	(one line when clean) and surfaces remote changes earlier:
842	
843	```
844	vc-x1 sync --check                    # dual-repo workspace, verify
845	vc-x1 sync --no-check                 # apply (rebase / fast-forward)
846	vc-x1 sync --check -R .               # single-repo project
847	vc-x1 sync --check --quiet            # silent; exit code signals result
848	```
849	
850	Bots and scripts must pass `--check` or `--no-check` explicitly —
851	defaults can shift, explicit flags lock in the contract. Interactive
852	use can take the default (which is `--check`).
853	
854	Output shape:
855	
856	- **Clean**: one line — `sync: N repos, all bookmarks up-to-date`.
857	  Note: scope is bookmark-vs-remote tracking, not working-copy
858	  cleanliness — `@` may have uncommitted changes; sync doesn't
859	  speak to that. Proceed.
860	- **Action needed** (`behind` / `diverged`) under `--check`:
861	  per-repo fetch + state lines, then a fatal
862	  `sync: N repos need action — resolve with vc-x1 sync --no-check
863	  and re-run`. Inspect, run `vc-x1 sync --no-check`, then proceed.
864	- **`--quiet`**: no output; exit code is the only signal.
865	
866	### After finalize: stop and wait
867	
868	After `vc-x1 finalize` is launched — **whether mid-session per-step
869	or at session end** — you **MUST NEVER** proceed to a next step, edit
870	files, run tools, or emit any text (prose, recaps, acknowledgements),
871	until the user explicitly directs you to continue. Treat finalize as
872	a hard stop for the whole turn. Any final words (e.g. "next is ...")
873	must be said in the approval prompt *before* executing finalize; the
874	finalize `Bash` call is the last thing in the turn and nothing
875	follows it.
876	
877	This holds even when the next step seems obvious (e.g. "next is
878	N+1" or "now I should bump the version and commit the release").
879	Wait. The user controls cadence — every push+finalize is a checkpoint
880	they may want to inspect, think about, hand off, or take a break at.
881	Auto-proceeding bypasses that checkpoint and produces unwanted writes
882	between finalize and the next explicit instruction.
883	
884	Exceptions to this rule may emerge later but are not authorized at
885	this stage. Until told otherwise, treat as absolute.
886	
887	### Late changes after push
888	
889	If the app repo needs a tweak after `push-app` succeeded (e.g.
890	updating CLAUDE.md or memory), the commit is immutable. Use
891	`--ignore-immutable` to squash the changes into `@-` — the
892	bookmark moves with the rewritten commit — then re-push:
893	
894	```
895	jj squash --ignore-immutable -R .
896	jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .
897	```
898	
899	If you squash somewhere other than `@-`, add
900	`jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <target> -R .` between those
901	two commands so the bookmark lands on the rewritten commit.
902	
903	`.bot` is also mutable via this pattern when needed, though
904	push's `finalize-claude` stage normally handles trailing session
905	writes so you rarely hit this case there.
906	
907	### Manual finalize fallback
908	
909	If push exited before `finalize-claude` (e.g. `--no-finalize`
910	was set, or a failure between `push-app` and `finalize-claude`),
911	run finalize by hand:
912	
913	```
914	vc-x1 finalize --repo .bot --squash --push <bookmark> --delay 10 --detach --log /tmp/vc-x1-finalize.log
915	```
916	
917	**Nothing should happen after finalize** — no memory writes, no
918	tool calls, no additional output. If any work is done after
919	finalize, run finalize again so the trailing writes are captured.
920	Do **not** echo or restate the finalize output — the Bash tool
921	already displays it.
922	
923	**Clear push's saved state after any out-of-band recovery** —
924	manual `vc-x1 finalize`, manual `jj squash --ignore-immutable`
925	+ force-push, etc., all leave `.vc-x1/push-state.toml` pointing
926	at a now-stale halt point. Either `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml`
927	or run `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --restart` (which clears and
928	restarts in one go) before the next `vc-x1 push`. Otherwise
929	push resumes from a bogus stage and can falsely declare
930	success.
